item.title: Quebecor makes cash-and-stock offer for Telus worth $31 billion
item.description: Quebecor Inc. is proposing a strategic combination with Telus Corp. in a cash-and-stock deal valued at about $31 billion.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: MONTREAL — Quebecor Inc. is proposing a merger with Telus Corp. in a cash-and-stock deal valued at about $31 billion, but competition concerns could stand in the way of a potential transaction. The Montreal-based company said Monday the proposed deal would combine complementary networks, spectrum and operations to boost investment capacity and create a more competitive company. Quebecor said it made a non-binding proposal to Telus on June 26 to serve as the basis for negotiations and then submitted what it called an “enhanced proposal” on Nov. 9. Under the offer, Telus shareholders would receive $6.35 in cash and 0.17 class B shares of Quebecor for each Telus share. Quebecor said the bid is worth $19.45 per share based on its closing share price on Friday. Telus shares closed at $12.14 on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Friday, while Quebecor’s class B shares closed at $77.06. Quebecor estimates the proposed takeover would create around $160 million in annual operating cost savings and $235 million in annual capital savings, on top of Telus’ recently announced goal of achieving approximately $900 million in savings per year moving forward from the end of 2028. It said those efficiencies would lead to more investment capacity at the combined company, which would support new spending on network upgrades, integration with Canadian satellite networks, service enhancements. It would also go toward the deployment of artificial intelligence, data centres and advanced connectivity infrastructure. Telus said its board of directors has formed a special committee of independent directors to review and evaluate the Quebecor proposal. Telus chair John Manley said the special committee is conducting a thorough review as well as exploring other strategic alternatives. “To date, this review has surfaced a number of significant risks associated with Quebecor’s proposal, including the fact that more than four months after its initial proposal, Quebecor has yet to explain how what it is proposing could be approved under the current telecom regulatory framework,” Manley said in a statement. “That said, we are prepared to continue our engagement with Quebecor and its advisers, as well as government and applicable regulatory authorities, in respect of the concerns raised.” A potential deal would face significant hurdles, said Scotiabank analyst Maher Yaghi, pointing to likely reviews by the Competition Bureau, the CRTC and Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada. He said additional federal reviews or approvals could also be required “given the strategic nature of Canadian telecommunications infrastructure.” Telus noted that even if such a deal received multiple regulatory approvals, it may be subject to certain conditions that “materially affect the combined company.”  It said a prolonged regulatory review process “would inevitably impose significant demands on Telus’ management and employees, create uncertainty for Telus, its customers, employees, shareholders, and other stakeholders, and constrain Telus’ ability to pursue and execute its strategic plan.” If a merger between Quebecor and Telus moved forward, it would be the largest takeover in Canada’s telecommunications sector since Rogers Communications Inc. purchased Shaw in 2023. As part of that $26-billion takeover, Quebecor’s Videotron subsidiary acquired Freedom Mobile from Shaw. Rogers and Shaw agreed to sell Freedom to Videotron for $2.85 billion in an attempt to ease competition concerns raised by the original proposal. Both of those transactions came with a list conditions meant to protect competition in the telecom sector. They included Rogers establishing a second headquarters in Calgary and adding 3,000 new jobs based in Western Canada that it must maintain for at least 10 years. Rogers was also required to spend billions to expand 5G coverage and additional network services, as well as to connect rural, remote and Indigenous communities. Videotron was required to offer plans at least 20 per cent lower than its competitors and spend $150 million over two years to upgrade Freedom Mobile’s network. It is also restricted from transferring any Freedom Mobile licences for a decade. Quebecor said that it “has fully performed the undertakings it made” to Ottawa since that deal, while demonstrating its ability “to combine growth, pro-consumer pricing and innovation.”  It noted that wireless prices fell 35.4 per cent in the three years following the acquisition of Freedom, according to Statistics Canada. “Providing Canadians with a stronger competitor, capable of investing more, while continuing to offer wider choice, including by maintaining the Telus brands, as well as healthy competition and real value, will remain at the core of the combined company’s DNA,” Quebecor said. Combining two of Canada’s four largest wireless service providers “would undo the competitive structure regulators set up when they required Freedom to be divested as part of the Rogers-Shaw approval,” Scotiabank’s Yaghi said in a note. “Without meaningful remedies, the deal runs against the government policy intent behind the Freedom transaction,” he said, adding that approval could be contingent on Quebecor offering “significant concessions to the government” to keep telecom prices low. “Regulatory decisions will make or break the deal, not price. If Quebecor is not ready to let go of Freedom Mobile, we believe this deal has a low chance of going through.” Quebecor’s share price fell about 14 per cent or $10.44 to $66.62 in morning trading. Telus’ share price jumped about 12 per cent or $1.46 to $13.60. --- Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

item.title: Canaccord Genuity selling British wealth management business, signs go-private deal
item.description: Canaccord Genuity Group Inc. has signed a deal to sell its wealth management business in the United Kingdom and become a private company.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Canaccord Genuity Group Inc. has signed a deal to sell its wealth management business in the United Kingdom and become a private company. Under the agreement, private equity investors Centerbridge Partners LP and Mubadala Investment Co. PJSC will buy the British wealth management operations in a deal that values the business at about 1.17 billion pounds. Meanwhile, a company led by Canaccord Genuity chair and CEO Dan Daviau will acquire the rest of the company’s business in a go-private transaction. Canaccord Genuity shareholders are expected to receive a cash payment of $7.45 per share, plus 4.15 pounds per share from the sale of wealth management business in the United Kingdom. The company valued the total offer at $15.27 per share, based on the exchange rates on Friday. It said the sale of the British wealth management business is expected to go ahead regardless of the completion of the go-private transaction. Shares of Canaccord were trading up one per cent at $14.97 at midday Monday. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

item.title: TC Energy plans to grow Alberta pipeline network to serve oilsands, power plants
item.description: TC Energy Corp. has announced plans to expand its Alberta natural gas pipeline network to get more supply to the oilsands region.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: CALGARY — TC Energy Corp. has announced plans to expand its Alberta natural gas pipeline network to get more supply to the oilsands region. It’s proposing a roughly 370-kilometre, 48-inch west-to-east pipeline called Alberta Growth Connector, which would add an initial one billion cubic feet per day of new capacity. That project would be part of a broader plan to grow its NGTL system, which has been in operation for almost 70 years and forms a vast web stretching throughout Alberta and into northeastern British Columbia. TC is projecting total demand on NGTL will increase by about a quarter to 18 billion cubic feet per day in 2031. More than 60 per cent of the forecast increase is expected to come from the oilsands, power generation and data centres. The growth plan could also include additional pipeline loops and compressor units to boost throughput on the existing system. “Our approach is deliberate and disciplined: leverage our existing infrastructure, align investment with customer commitments and advance projects that meet our risk and return requirements,” chief executive François Poirier said in a news release Monday. --- Lauren Krugel, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.

item.title: Tiff Macklem to step down as Bank of Canada governor at end of his term
item.description: The Bank of Canada says Tiff Macklem will not seek a second term as governor and plans to step down when his current run expires on June 2, 2027.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA — The Bank of Canada says Tiff Macklem will not seek a second term as governor and plans to step down when his current run expires on June 2, 2027.    The central bank’s board of directors says it has started a search process to select the next governor. “It has been the highlight of my career to serve as the 10th governor of the Bank of Canada,” Macklem said in a news release Monday. He said his tenure has come as Canada navigates a world that is more fragmented and shock-prone. “The bank has faced these challenges by acting decisively, by using sound judgment in the face of uncertainty, and by serving Canadians with humility and a steadfast commitment to its mandate,” he said.  Macklem was named governor in May 2020 and took over the job in June of that year, during the early days of the pandemic. The central bank said the recruitment process is expected to be completed by spring 2027. The board’s choice will be subject to approval by the minister of finance and the federal cabinet. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 16, 2026.
